case_study_insert.main_stem: Garrow Turbine Components (GTB) is a partnership in the precision turbine-casting sector in South Wales, employing a workforce of 72. Founded in 2003 by Gwen Garrow, it casts turbine blades and hot-section components for energy and aerospace clients and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. GTB plans to invest $880,000 in a new vacuum-casting furnace, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $260,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a unit and a selling price of $18.00, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. GTB faces an operational problem: the casting defect rate has reached 5.1% and skilled-worker absence is rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The South Wales foundry poured 9,800 turbine-casting units last quarter at a defect rate of 5.1%, up from 3.2% a year earlier. Customer quality complaints rose from 19 to 37 per month. Average delivery time lengthened to 16 days from 10 days. A survey of 220 energy and aerospace buyers found that 59% would pay up to $1.10 more for certified low-defect castings, and 46% rank quality assurance first. A skills audit shows 21 of 72 staff need furnace-control retraining; on-the-job mentoring is offered, external courses cost $940 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, raising borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $13.20 to $14.01 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills. (3) Nickel alloy and cobalt input costs have risen 12.7% year-on-year, while turbine component demand grew 3.4%.

questions.question_text: GTB plans to finance part of its $880,000 vacuum-casting furnace with a $480,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for GTB of using the $400,000 retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest or capital repayments, so GTB avoids extra debt service on top of fixed costs of $260,000 a year while the $880,000 furnace is installed. That protects cash flow and helps absorb the 6.1% wage rise and the 12.7% rise in nickel and cobalt costs without raising the $18.00 selling price. Cash kept from lenders can fund the 21 staff needing furnace-control retraining.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps the furnace free of lender security and covenants, so Gwen Garrow and the partners retain control of casting operations without a bank dictating terms. Unlike the $480,000 bank loan, there is no repossession risk if aerospace orders weaken, and the $400,000 can be applied flexibly alongside the borrowing rather than tied to a rigid repayment timetable. This flexibility matters with a 5.1% defect rate and complaints already up from 19 to 37 a month. The $400,000 can also be drawn as needed rather than all at once, which suits a foundry facing a 5.1% defect rate.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to GTB and its $880,000 financing decision.

questions.question_text: GTB is promoting its certified low-defect turbine castings. Consider advertising in aerospace journals, exhibiting at an energy-industry exhibition, or using social media aimed at procurement engineers. Which should GTB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Advertising in aerospace journals: Print adverts would reach design and procurement engineers at energy and aerospace firms and add credibility to the certified low-defect claim. The drawback is that campaigns are costly and poorly targeted; many readers will not buy turbine castings, and a partnership with $260,000 fixed costs and an $880,000 furnace cannot afford much wasted spend with no measurable enquiries.

Energy-industry exhibition: A stand lets engineers inspect sample castings and question GTB about the 5.1% defect rate and the new vacuum furnace. It matches the 46% of surveyed buyers who rank quality assurance first, because certificates and finish can be shown on the spot. The limits are stand cost, a short event window and the need for prompt follow-up with the 220 buyers in the survey.

Social media aimed at procurement engineers: Targeted posts can reach the 59% of buyers who would pay $1.10 more for certified low-defect castings at low cost, with measurable clicks and quick feedback. It suits a 72-employee firm, but engineers usually require physical inspection and certification evidence before switching supplier, so social media alone may generate interest rather than firm orders.

Recommendation: GTB should choose the energy-industry exhibition as the primary channel, supported by low-cost social media follow-up. Inspection of castings best overcomes worry about the 5.1% defect rate and directly reaches the buyers in the 46% who rank quality first. Aerospace journals are rejected as untargeted and unmeasurable for a small partnership; social media alone is rejected because technical buyers need physical evidence, so it should support rather than replace the exhibition.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to GTB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of GTB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of GTB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why journals and social media alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: GTB's casting defect rate is 5.1% and absence is rising. Explain two benefits for GTB of replacing autocratic leadership with a more democratic style in its foundry.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership would give the 72 staff a voice in running the new vacuum-casting furnace, raising job satisfaction and helping cut the 5.1% defect rate. Foundry workers know the pouring settings best, so their suggestions can reduce defects without further capital spending on the $880,000 furnace, while being consulted should improve attendance and reduce the rising skilled-worker absence. Maslow's esteem needs are met by involvement, so motivation rises without extra pay.

Point 2: Involvement builds commitment and lowers labour turnover in the hierarchical structure, cutting the need to retrain the 21 staff identified in the skills audit at $940 each. Herzberg would treat responsibility as a motivator, so workers take greater care over casting finish. Better upward communication also means furnace problems are reported sooner, protecting output of 70,000 castings and the $8.00 contribution on each $18.00 unit while the new furnace beds in and the 16-day delivery time is shortened.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GTB's defect rate, absence, workforce and retraining costs.

questions.question_text: GTB must retrain 21 staff to operate the new vacuum-casting furnace. Consider on-the-job mentoring or external courses at $940 per employee. Which should GTB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job mentoring: Mentoring at the South Wales foundry is specific to GTB's furnace and casting standards, avoids the $940 per person fee for 21 staff, a saving of $19,740 (21 × $940), and keeps workers productive while learning. That protects the 9,800 units poured last quarter and helps tackle the 5.1% defect rate. The drawbacks are that mentors are taken off their own work, bad habits can spread, and there is no external certificate, which matters when 46% of buyers rank quality assurance first.

External courses: At $940 each, 21 staff cost $19,740, modest against the $880,000 investment and simpler to schedule away from the foundry. Outside providers bring current furnace-control theory and a recognised certificate, useful with rising absence and a hierarchical structure that values formal standards, and supportive of the 59% who would pay $1.10 more for certified low-defect castings. However, staff leave the foundry floor, reducing capacity on the new furnace, and generic content may not match GTB's exact pouring conditions, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: GTB should choose on-the-job mentoring first, adding short external modules for lead operators. Mentoring is cheaper, furnace-specific and avoids output loss while defects are 5.1% and absence is rising. Full external training is rejected because sending 21 of 72 staff off-site and spending $19,740 would slow commissioning of the $880,000 furnace and still need on-site reinforcement; certification can be added once the furnace is stable and the 16-day delivery time is reduced. The $19,740 saved also helps cover the $260,000 fixed costs while the 16-day delivery time is shortened.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to GTB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of GTB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of GTB with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and furnace relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GTB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $260,000 ÷ ($18.00 − $10.00) = $260,000 ÷ $8.00 = 32,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 32,500 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $18.00 − $10.00 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GTB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 32,500-unit break-even output with actual output of 70,000 castings gives a margin of safety of 37,500 units, showing room to fill the $880,000 vacuum furnace before losses occur.
2. Contribution of $8.00 a casting lets GTB test the $1.10 premium for certified low-defect castings; if the 59% of buyers accept it, contribution would rise to $9.10 and the $260,000 fixed costs would be covered sooner.
3. Fixed costs of $260,000 and $8.00 contribution indicate the extra volume needed to service the $480,000 bank loan, so the partners can set sales targets for energy and aerospace clients.
4. Average total cost of $13.71 a casting ($260,000 ÷ 70,000 = $3.71 plus $10.00) can be tracked against the 5.1% defect rate to judge whether the vacuum furnace is reducing rework and to monitor the $10.00 variable cost as nickel and cobalt prices rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 32,500 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 70,000-unit output; certified-casting premium modelling; loan-service volume for the $480,000 borrowing; and average total cost of $13.71 to monitor defects.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GTB's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GTB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.83 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.03 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.18 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.45 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $130,000 inventories + $180,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $365,000; 2025 current assets = $112,000 + $205,000 + $78,000 = $395,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 = $365,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.83 and 2025 = $395,000 ÷ $195,000 = 2.03. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($365,000 − $130,000) ÷ $200,000 = $235,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.18; 2025 = ($395,000 − $112,000) ÷ $195,000 = $283,000 ÷ $195,000 = 1.45.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened clearly. The current ratio rose from 1.83 to 2.03 as current liabilities fell from $200,000 to $195,000 while current assets grew from $365,000 to $395,000. The acid test improved even more, from 1.18 to 1.45, so GTB can meet short-term debts without relying on selling inventory, important while it services a $480,000 bank loan and buys an $880,000 furnace. Cash rose from $55,000 to $78,000 and inventories fell from $130,000 to $112,000, both helpful. The caution is trade receivables climbing from $180,000 to $205,000; with a 5.1% defect rate, any dispute over casting quality could delay collection and weaken the position.

Conclusion: GTB's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.83 to 2.03) and the acid test (1.18 to 1.45) show stronger short-term solvency, and the acid test is the stronger evidence because it excludes the $112,000 of inventories and still rises. The main residual risk is the $205,000 of trade receivables, so the partners should tighten credit control while proceeding with the furnace investment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GTB of introducing quality-assurance certification for its 5.1% defect-rate problem.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Formal quality assurance would attack the 5.1% casting defect rate at source and support the certification that 46% of surveyed buyers rank first. It also lets GTB pursue the 59% who would pay $1.10 more for certified low-defect castings, protecting the $8.00 contribution on each $18.00 unit and strengthening returns from the $880,000 furnace. Fewer defects also cut rework and help shorten the 16-day delivery time.

Disadvantage: Setting up certification and training the 21 staff may slow output of 70,000 castings and add costs on top of $260,000 fixed costs. The insert gives no figure for inspection cost or rework savings, so the net benefit cannot be quantified, and an autocratic hierarchical culture may resist the staff involvement that quality assurance requires, limiting its effect on the defect rate. With complaints already up from 19 to 37 a month and absence rising, extra procedures could lengthen delivery further and weaken the 46% quality-focused segment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GTB's defect rate, research data and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 12.7% rise in nickel alloy and cobalt input costs will affect GTB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If GTB's $480,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by the 0.75 percentage-point rise × $480,000 = $3,600 a year (0.0075 × $480,000). That is small next to fixed costs of $260,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Higher rates may also make energy and aerospace clients delay orders, but GTB can largely remove the direct risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.1%, to $14.01 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 72 but not hours worked, individual pay or how many are on the minimum, so a defensible annual wage bill cannot be invented. The figure that can be derived is labour productivity: 70,000 castings ÷ 72 staff = 972.22 castings per worker. If that holds, the rise is manageable; if the 5.1% defect rate or rising absence reduces output, unit labour cost climbs and the $8.00 contribution per casting narrows. The effect is real but cannot be precisely quantified from the data.

Input cost inflation (12.7% on nickel and cobalt): The insert does not decompose the $10.00 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled upper bound is honest: if the whole $10.00 rose 12.7%, it adds 12.7% × $10.00 = $1.27 per casting, and across 70,000 castings a year that is $88,900 (70,000 × $1.27). Even a partial rise compounds over all output and cuts contribution below $8.00, though the $1.10 certified low-defect premium found in the survey could recover part of it.

Conclusion: The 12.7% rise in nickel and cobalt inputs will have the greatest impact. Its $88,900 bound far exceeds the $3,600 interest effect, it applies to every one of the 70,000 castings, and it directly erodes the $8.00 contribution needed to cover $260,000 fixed costs and service the $480,000 loan. The interest rise is small and hedgeable by fixing the rate; the wage rise cannot be quantified from the insert and can be partly offset through productivity of 972.22 castings per worker.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to GTB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GTB with shown calculations where data allow.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of GTB using only shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgment.
